Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. Verify Now Blog > How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity high-speed PCB design via stub Anyone involved in high-speed PCB design has probably heard this rule of thumb: minimize vias in high-speed routing whenever possible. But many engineers know they should do this without fully understanding why. Some consider a via simply a “wire” and assume a few extra vias will not matter. Others believe that as long as the impedance is controlled, everything will be fine. It is often only after the board comes back for testing—with a collapsed eye diagram, increased bit errors, or EMC test failures—that they realize those seemingly insignificant vias may be part of the problem. A PCB via is one of the structures in a high-speed link that can introduce impedance discontinuities and parasitic effects. It introduces parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, via stubs, and changes in the return-current path. As signal edges become faster, these effects become increasingly important to signal integrity. 1. What Parasitic Parameters Does a PCB Via Introduce? Many engineers think of a via as simply a “vertical wire.” At high frequencies, however, a PCB via is actually a three-dimensional interconnect structure with parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, and transmission-line effects. Parasitic Capacitance (C_via) Parasitic capacitance forms between the via pad and the surrounding reference plane, such as a ground or power plane. Its value depends on factors including the via pad, anti-pad, distance to the reference plane, and dielectric material. T: Length of the via passing through the reference plane D₁: Via pad diameter D₂: Anti-pad diameter εr: Relative dielectric constant In typical structures, via parasitic capacitance is usually on the order of several hundred femtofarads (fF). Parasitic capacitance lowers the local impedance around the via and, together with other parasitic parameters, creates an impedance discontinuity that can cause signal reflections. Parasitic Inductance (L_via) The copper barrel and the vertical current path of a via also introduce parasitic inductance. h: Via length in the vertical direction d: Via diameter For a typical 1.6 mm PCB with common via dimensions, the parasitic inductance can be around the 1 nH range. Parasitic inductance increases the local impedance around the via and interacts with parasitic capacitance to affect high-speed signals. If the return path is not properly controlled during layer transitions, the additional loop inductance can also increase EMI radiation. Combined Effects of Capacitance and Inductance The actual electrical behavior of a via is not determined by capacitance or inductance alone. Multiple parasitic effects work together. By properly optimizing via dimensions, pads, and anti-pads, the impedance discontinuity can be reduced to some extent. However, when a relatively long via stub is present, the frequency response of the via structure can still exhibit significant resonance. 2. Why Is Via Stub a Major Concern? （Through Via and Via Stub） This is one of the easily overlooked issues in high-speed PCB design. When a signal travels through a through-hole via from the top layer to an inner layer, such as from the Top Layer to L3, the unused portion of the plated hole extending from L3 to the bottom layer L10 becomes a via stub. The Physical Nature of a Via Stub A via stub is essentially an open-ended transmission-line section. At certain frequencies, it can produce a significant resonance. The resonant frequency can be approximately expressed as: c: Speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) L_stub: Via stub length εr: Relative dielectric constant When the via stub's resonant frequency enters the main frequency range of the signal, it can cause a pronounced notch in insertion loss. This can result in signal attenuation and waveform distortion and, in severe cases, lead to eye-diagram closure. Therefore, for high-speed signals, via stub length can be more important than considering the parasitic capacitance and inductance of the via alone. 3. Why Does a PCB Via Cause Impedance Discontinuity? （Via Impedance Discontinuities and Reflections） The impedance of a via, Z_via, is usually not exactly the same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line, Z₀. For example, a common target impedance for a high-speed single-ended signal is 50 Ω. When a signal transitions from a transmission line into a via structure with a different impedance, part of the signal is reflected. The reflection coefficient can be expressed as: Γ = (Z_via - Z₀) / (Z_via + Z₀) If Z_via = 40 Ω and Z₀ = 50 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.11. If Z_via = 30 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.25. This shows that a larger impedance mismatch between the via and transmission line generally results in stronger local reflections. For this reason, via optimization in high-speed PCB design is not simply about avoiding vias. The goal is to minimize the impedance discontinuity between the via structure and the transmission line. 4. Why Should You Consider the Return Path During Layer Transitions? （Layer Transition and Return Current Path） A via can affect not only the signal itself but also its return-current path. When a signal changes layers, its reference plane may also change. For example, a signal may transition between routing layers associated with different reference planes. If there is no suitable return path near the layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer route, creating a larger current loop. This can lead to: Increased loop inductance Increased EMI radiation Degraded signal integrity Increased crosstalk Therefore, high-speed via design needs to consider not only how the signal travels, but also how its return current flows back. 5. When Do Vias Significantly Affect High-Speed Signals? Many engineers have the same question: if the parasitic parameters of a via are so small, can a via really affect a high-speed signal? When evaluating the impact of a PCB via, data rate alone is not enough. Signal rise time, via propagation delay, and via stub resonance also need to be considered. Rise Time vs. Via Propagation Delay The propagation delay of a via can be approximately expressed as: For a typical via with L = 1.2 nH and C = 0.4 pF: This time scale is usually relatively small. Therefore, for many common high-speed digital signals, the impact of the via's lumped L/C parameters alone may not be as significant as the resonance caused by a long via stub. However, as signal edges become faster, via geometry, impedance discontinuity, and return-path design become increasingly important to signal integrity. Via Stub Resonance vs. Signal Spectrum Instead of using data rate alone as the criterion, it is more important to consider whether the via stub resonance falls within the main frequency range of the signal. When these frequencies become close, the via stub can create a significant notch in the frequency response, affecting insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, there is no single data-rate threshold that determines whether a via will cause problems. The actual design should consider data rate, rise time, via stub length, Nyquist frequency, and channel loss together. 6. Why Is a Via a Weak Point in a High-Speed Link? A PCB trace can be designed as a relatively continuous transmission structure by controlling parameters such as trace width, dielectric thickness, and copper thickness. A via, however, has to perform a three-dimensional transition over a very short distance. As a result, a single PCB via may introduce: Parasitic capacitance Parasitic inductance Impedance discontinuity Via stub resonance Return-path discontinuity The trace is like a “highway,” while the via is more like a combination of a “toll station + sharp turn + dead-end road.” A single via may not cause a significant problem by itself. However, when multiple discontinuities appear along the same high-speed link, their effects can accumulate and eventually appear as increased insertion loss, return loss, or eye-diagram degradation. 7. How Can You Reduce the Impact of Vias? Minimize Unnecessary Vias High-speed signals should avoid unnecessary layer transitions and multiple vias within a short routing distance. During BGA fanout, optimize the component placement and routing-layer strategy to minimize the number of layer transitions for critical high-speed signals. Use Back Drilling For high-speed SerDes links and other applications with demanding signal integrity requirements, if the via stub enters the effective frequency range of the signal, back drilling can be used to remove most of the unused plated barrel. The primary purpose of back drilling is to shorten the via stub and reduce the impact of via stub resonance on high-speed signals. The required back-drilling depth and remaining stub length should be determined based on the PCB stackup, signal characteristics, and manufacturing capabilities rather than a fixed data-rate threshold. Optimize Via Anti-Pads The anti-pad affects the parasitic capacitance between the via and the reference plane. Anti-pad too small: Higher parasitic capacitance, which may reduce the local impedance. Anti-pad too large: Although it can reduce some parasitic capacitance, it may also create a larger opening in the reference plane and affect the return path. Therefore, via anti-pad dimensions should be optimized based on via size, stackup, reference-plane spacing, and target impedance, rather than using a fixed dimension. Add Ground Return Vias During a high-speed layer transition, ground vias can be placed near the signal via to provide a shorter, lower-inductance return-current path. For differential signals, the ground vias should also be arranged as symmetrically as practical to avoid significant differences in the return environment of the two traces. Optimize Via Dimensions Within the limits of manufacturing capability, via diameter, pad size, and via length can be optimized to reduce parasitic effects. For example: A smaller drill diameter can reduce some parasitic effects. A smaller pad can reduce coupling to the reference plane. A shorter via can reduce parasitic inductance and via stub length. However, smaller is not always better. Very small vias can increase PCB manufacturing difficulty and cost. Choose an Appropriate Stackup High-speed signal layers should be placed close to continuous reference planes to maintain strong coupling between the signal and its return path. For high-density, high-speed designs, blind vias, buried vias, and HDI structures can also be used to shorten the via length and reduce the impact of through-hole via stubs. Conclusion A via is not simply a “vertical wire.” In high-speed PCB design , it is a complex three-dimensional interconnect structure involving parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, impedance discontinuity, via stub resonance, and return-path changes. In many cases, the lumped parasitic parameters of a single via are not the dominant source of signal degradation. However, when a via creates a significant impedance discontinuity or its via stub resonance enters the effective frequency range of the signal, it can have a noticeable impact on insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, the key question in high-speed PCB design is not simply whether a via can be used, but: Will this via structure introduce an unacceptable discontinuity within the effective frequency range of the target signal? Minimizing unnecessary vias, controlling via stub length, using back drilling or HDI structures when appropriate, and maintaining a continuous return path are all effective ways to improve signal integrity in high-speed links. Verify Now Blog > How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity high-speed PCB design via stub Anyone involved in high-speed PCB design has probably heard this rule of thumb: minimize vias in high-speed routing whenever possible. But many engineers know they should do this without fully understanding why. Some consider a via simply a “wire” and assume a few extra vias will not matter. Others believe that as long as the impedance is controlled, everything will be fine. It is often only after the board comes back for testing—with a collapsed eye diagram, increased bit errors, or EMC test failures—that they realize those seemingly insignificant vias may be part of the problem. A PCB via is one of the structures in a high-speed link that can introduce impedance discontinuities and parasitic effects. It introduces parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, via stubs, and changes in the return-current path. As signal edges become faster, these effects become increasingly important to signal integrity. 1. What Parasitic Parameters Does a PCB Via Introduce? Many engineers think of a via as simply a “vertical wire.” At high frequencies, however, a PCB via is actually a three-dimensional interconnect structure with parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, and transmission-line effects. Parasitic Capacitance (C_via) Parasitic capacitance forms between the via pad and the surrounding reference plane, such as a ground or power plane. Its value depends on factors including the via pad, anti-pad, distance to the reference plane, and dielectric material. T: Length of the via passing through the reference plane D₁: Via pad diameter D₂: Anti-pad diameter εr: Relative dielectric constant In typical structures, via parasitic capacitance is usually on the order of several hundred femtofarads (fF). Parasitic capacitance lowers the local impedance around the via and, together with other parasitic parameters, creates an impedance discontinuity that can cause signal reflections. Parasitic Inductance (L_via) The copper barrel and the vertical current path of a via also introduce parasitic inductance. h: Via length in the vertical direction d: Via diameter For a typical 1.6 mm PCB with common via dimensions, the parasitic inductance can be around the 1 nH range. Parasitic inductance increases the local impedance around the via and interacts with parasitic capacitance to affect high-speed signals. If the return path is not properly controlled during layer transitions, the additional loop inductance can also increase EMI radiation. Combined Effects of Capacitance and Inductance The actual electrical behavior of a via is not determined by capacitance or inductance alone. Multiple parasitic effects work together. By properly optimizing via dimensions, pads, and anti-pads, the impedance discontinuity can be reduced to some extent. However, when a relatively long via stub is present, the frequency response of the via structure can still exhibit significant resonance. 2. Why Is Via Stub a Major Concern? （Through Via and Via Stub） This is one of the easily overlooked issues in high-speed PCB design. When a signal travels through a through-hole via from the top layer to an inner layer, such as from the Top Layer to L3, the unused portion of the plated hole extending from L3 to the bottom layer L10 becomes a via stub. The Physical Nature of a Via Stub A via stub is essentially an open-ended transmission-line section. At certain frequencies, it can produce a significant resonance. The resonant frequency can be approximately expressed as: c: Speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) L_stub: Via stub length εr: Relative dielectric constant When the via stub's resonant frequency enters the main frequency range of the signal, it can cause a pronounced notch in insertion loss. This can result in signal attenuation and waveform distortion and, in severe cases, lead to eye-diagram closure. Therefore, for high-speed signals, via stub length can be more important than considering the parasitic capacitance and inductance of the via alone. 3. Why Does a PCB Via Cause Impedance Discontinuity? （Via Impedance Discontinuities and Reflections） The impedance of a via, Z_via, is usually not exactly the same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line, Z₀. For example, a common target impedance for a high-speed single-ended signal is 50 Ω. When a signal transitions from a transmission line into a via structure with a different impedance, part of the signal is reflected. The reflection coefficient can be expressed as: Γ = (Z_via - Z₀) / (Z_via + Z₀) If Z_via = 40 Ω and Z₀ = 50 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.11. If Z_via = 30 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.25. This shows that a larger impedance mismatch between the via and transmission line generally results in stronger local reflections. For this reason, via optimization in high-speed PCB design is not simply about avoiding vias. The goal is to minimize the impedance discontinuity between the via structure and the transmission line. 4. Why Should You Consider the Return Path During Layer Transitions? （Layer Transition and Return Current Path） A via can affect not only the signal itself but also its return-current path. When a signal changes layers, its reference plane may also change. For example, a signal may transition between routing layers associated with different reference planes. If there is no suitable return path near the layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer route, creating a larger current loop. This can lead to: Increased loop inductance Increased EMI radiation Degraded signal integrity Increased crosstalk Therefore, high-speed via design needs to consider not only how the signal travels, but also how its return current flows back. 5. When Do Vias Significantly Affect High-Speed Signals? Many engineers have the same question: if the parasitic parameters of a via are so small, can a via really affect a high-speed signal? When evaluating the impact of a PCB via, data rate alone is not enough. Signal rise time, via propagation delay, and via stub resonance also need to be considered. Rise Time vs. Via Propagation Delay The propagation delay of a via can be approximately expressed as: For a typical via with L = 1.2 nH and C = 0.4 pF: This time scale is usually relatively small. Therefore, for many common high-speed digital signals, the impact of the via's lumped L/C parameters alone may not be as significant as the resonance caused by a long via stub. However, as signal edges become faster, via geometry, impedance discontinuity, and return-path design become increasingly important to signal integrity. Via Stub Resonance vs. Signal Spectrum Instead of using data rate alone as the criterion, it is more important to consider whether the via stub resonance falls within the main frequency range of the signal. When these frequencies become close, the via stub can create a significant notch in the frequency response, affecting insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, there is no single data-rate threshold that determines whether a via will cause problems. The actual design should consider data rate, rise time, via stub length, Nyquist frequency, and channel loss together. 6. Why Is a Via a Weak Point in a High-Speed Link? A PCB trace can be designed as a relatively continuous transmission structure by controlling parameters such as trace width, dielectric thickness, and copper thickness. A via, however, has to perform a three-dimensional transition over a very short distance. As a result, a single PCB via may introduce: Parasitic capacitance Parasitic inductance Impedance discontinuity Via stub resonance Return-path discontinuity The trace is like a “highway,” while the via is more like a combination of a “toll station + sharp turn + dead-end road.” A single via may not cause a significant problem by itself. However, when multiple discontinuities appear along the same high-speed link, their effects can accumulate and eventually appear as increased insertion loss, return loss, or eye-diagram degradation. 7. How Can You Reduce the Impact of Vias? Minimize Unnecessary Vias High-speed signals should avoid unnecessary layer transitions and multiple vias within a short routing distance. During BGA fanout, optimize the component placement and routing-layer strategy to minimize the number of layer transitions for critical high-speed signals. Use Back Drilling For high-speed SerDes links and other applications with demanding signal integrity requirements, if the via stub enters the effective frequency range of the signal, back drilling can be used to remove most of the unused plated barrel. The primary purpose of back drilling is to shorten the via stub and reduce the impact of via stub resonance on high-speed signals. The required back-drilling depth and remaining stub length should be determined based on the PCB stackup, signal characteristics, and manufacturing capabilities rather than a fixed data-rate threshold. Optimize Via Anti-Pads The anti-pad affects the parasitic capacitance between the via and the reference plane. Anti-pad too small: Higher parasitic capacitance, which may reduce the local impedance. Anti-pad too large: Although it can reduce some parasitic capacitance, it may also create a larger opening in the reference plane and affect the return path. Therefore, via anti-pad dimensions should be optimized based on via size, stackup, reference-plane spacing, and target impedance, rather than using a fixed dimension. Add Ground Return Vias During a high-speed layer transition, ground vias can be placed near the signal via to provide a shorter, lower-inductance return-current path. For differential signals, the ground vias should also be arranged as symmetrically as practical to avoid significant differences in the return environment of the two traces. Optimize Via Dimensions Within the limits of manufacturing capability, via diameter, pad size, and via length can be optimized to reduce parasitic effects. For example: A smaller drill diameter can reduce some parasitic effects. A smaller pad can reduce coupling to the reference plane. A shorter via can reduce parasitic inductance and via stub length. However, smaller is not always better. Very small vias can increase PCB manufacturing difficulty and cost. Choose an Appropriate Stackup High-speed signal layers should be placed close to continuous reference planes to maintain strong coupling between the signal and its return path. For high-density, high-speed designs, blind vias, buried vias, and HDI structures can also be used to shorten the via length and reduce the impact of through-hole via stubs. Conclusion A via is not simply a “vertical wire.” In high-speed PCB design , it is a complex three-dimensional interconnect structure involving parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, impedance discontinuity, via stub resonance, and return-path changes. In many cases, the lumped parasitic parameters of a single via are not the dominant source of signal degradation. However, when a via creates a significant impedance discontinuity or its via stub resonance enters the effective frequency range of the signal, it can have a noticeable impact on insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, the key question in high-speed PCB design is not simply whether a via can be used, but: Will this via structure introduce an unacceptable discontinuity within the effective frequency range of the target signal? Minimizing unnecessary vias, controlling via stub length, using back drilling or HDI structures when appropriate, and maintaining a continuous return path are all effective ways to improve signal integrity in high-speed links.
