events.before: Resources Data Centers Server Rack: Definition, Sizes, and Units Server Rack: Definition, Sizes, and Units Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 23 min read Published September 15, 2026 A server rack is a standardized enclosure designed to organize, mount, secure, and manage servers, networking devices, storage systems, and other Information Technology (IT) equipment inside data centers, server rooms, and network closets. Standardized rack dimensions allow hardware from different manufacturers to fit within the same framework, improving equipment compatibility, airflow management, cable organization, and maintenance efficiency. Most enterprise server racks follow the Electronic Industries Alliance (EIA)-310 standard, which specifies a mounting width of 19 inches. Server racks are measured using rack units (U), where one rack unit equals 1.75 inches (44.45 millimeters (mm)) of vertical mounting space. Common rack heights range from compact 6U wall-mounted enclosures to 48U enterprise cabinets, while 42U remains the most widely deployed configuration in data centers. Server rack deployments support equipment organization, standardized hardware installation, power distribution, cable management, and cooling efficiency across enterprise, colocation, and hyperscale facilities. Rack selection depends on equipment size, weight capacity, cooling requirements, security needs, and future expansion plans. What Is a Server Rack? A server rack is a standardized metal frame built to hold servers, switches, patch panels, and other IT hardware in an organized vertical structure. Manufacturers construct racks from steel or aluminum, following the EIA-310 standard that sets a nominal mounting width of 19 inches. Rack height is measured in rack units, with 1U equal to 1.75 inches (44.45 mm), letting operators calculate equipment capacity before installation. Data centers, network closets, and office server rooms rely on racks to consolidate hardware, reduce cabling distance, and simplify power distribution. Mounting rails inside the frame support sliding or fixed installation of rack-mount servers, while vertical space above and below equipment accommodates cable management arms and blanking panels. Full-size racks commonly reach 42U to 48U, holding dozens of 1U or 2U servers within a single footprint. Open frame designs expose equipment directly to room airflow, while enclosed cabinets add doors, side panels, and locking mechanisms for physical security. Selection of a specific frame depends on floor space, cooling method, and equipment density planned for the deployment. What Is the Difference Between a Server Rack and a Data Rack? Server Rack and data rack terminology overlaps significantly across the IT industry, with vendors and technicians often using both terms for the same physical frame. The distinction between the two centers on scope, since data rack sometimes covers networking, storage, and telecom equipment beyond server hardware alone. The table below compares defining features, typical contents, and common applications for each term. Feature Server Rack Data Rack Typical Use Case Feature Primary Contents Server Rack Rack-mount servers, blade chassis Data Rack Servers, switches, storage arrays, patch panels Typical Use Case Server rack fits compute-focused deployments Feature Terminology Scope Server Rack Narrower, hardware-specific Data Rack Broader, covers mixed IT equipment Typical Use Case Data rack fits mixed network and storage rooms Feature Standard Sizing Server Rack 19-inch width, 42U to 48U height Data Rack 19-inch or 23-inch width, varies by industry Typical Use Case Telecom sites favor 23-inch data racks Feature Industry Usage Server Rack Common in data centers, cloud facilities Data Rack Common in telecom, enterprise IT closets Typical Use Case Terms used interchangeably in casual reference What Are Server Rack Units (U)? Rack units (U) measure vertical space inside a rack frame, with each U equal to 1.75 inches (44.45 mm) of mounting height. Manufacturers label server chassis, switches, and storage enclosures by U count, letting technicians match equipment to available rack space before ordering hardware. A 1U server occupies a single unit, a 2U chassis occupies two units, and full-size racks commonly span 42U to 48U in total height. Rack units matter because capacity planning, airflow design, and equipment compatibility depend on accurate U measurements. Miscalculating available U space leads to failed installations or wasted rack capacity, since a 4U chassis cannot fit inside a 2U opening regardless of width compatibility. Data center operators track U allocation across every rack to forecast growth, plan power distribution, and avoid overloading a single frame with equipment exceeding its rated capacity. Standardized U measurements let vendors design equipment compatible across different rack manufacturers, since the EIA-310 specification governs both width and unit height industry wide. What Are the Different Server Rack Types? Server Rack types vary by frame construction, physical security, and mounting method across data centers and IT facilities. Manufacturers group frames into open structures, enclosed structures, and specialty structures, each suited to different security and airflow requirements. Selection depends on floor space, access control, and environmental conditions present at the installation site. Server Rack types fall into the categories listed below. Open Structures: Open structures expose mounted equipment directly to room airflow, relying on two or four vertical posts without side panels. Frames in this category prioritize ventilation and low material cost over physical security. Open structures suit controlled-access facilities where airflow ranks above enclosure protection. Enclosed Structures: Enclosed structures surround equipment with side panels and lockable doors, adding a physical barrier against unauthorized access. Perforated panels maintain airflow while restricting tampering with installed hardware. Enclosed structures suit shared offices and mixed-use facilities requiring equipment protection. Specialty Structures: Specialty structures address unique installation conditions, including wall mounting, seismic reinforcement, or portable deployment. Frame dimensions and bracing differ from standard floor-mounted racks to meet site-specific constraints. Specialty structures suit branch offices, earthquake zones, and temporary or mobile deployments. What Are the Most Common Server Rack Types? The most common Server Rack types include open frame racks, enclosed cabinets, wall-mounted racks, and seismic racks, each suited to different security and installation needs. Selection depends on facility access control, available floor space, and regional building requirements. Facilities combine multiple types across a single deployment based on equipment sensitivity and location. The most common Server Rack types are listed below. Open Frame Racks: Open frame racks expose mounted equipment directly to room airflow, using two or four vertical posts without side panels or doors. Technicians access cabling and hardware from any side, simplifying installation and maintenance in controlled environments. Data centers with restricted room access commonly deploy open frames to maximize airflow and lower equipment cost. Enclosed Cabinets: Enclosed cabinets surround mounted equipment with side panels, front, and rear doors, adding locking mechanisms for physical security. Perforated doors allow airflow while blocking unauthorized access to installed hardware. Office environments and shared facilities favor enclosed cabinets to protect equipment from dust, tampering, and unauthorized removal. Wall-Mounted Racks: Wall-mounted racks attach directly to a wall surface, holding smaller equipment loads in space-limited environments. Capacity typically ranges from 4U to 24U, supporting switches, patch panels, and small servers. Branch offices and network closets rely on wall-mounted racks when floor space remains unavailable for a full-size frame. Seismic Racks: Seismic racks add reinforced framing, bracing, and anchoring points designed to withstand earthquake activity without equipment displacement. Construction follows standards including Telcordia GR-63-CORE, part of the Network Equipment-Building System (NEBS) compliance framework. Facilities located in earthquake-prone regions install seismic racks to protect hardware and maintain uptime during seismic events. How do rack cabinets and open frame racks compare? Rack cabinets and open frame racks differ primarily in airflow management, physical security, and equipment accessibility across a facility. Cabinets add enclosed panels and doors, trading airflow volume for protection against dust and unauthorized access. Open frames maximize airflow and access at the cost of physical security, favoring environments with restricted room entry. The table below compares defining characteristics between the two frame types. Feature Rack Cabinet Open Frame Rack Best Use Case Feature Airflow Rack Cabinet Supported by perforated doors; solid doors require forced airflow Open Frame Rack Unrestricted, relies on room airflow Best Use Case Open frame favors high-density cooling needs Feature Security Rack Cabinet Lockable doors, side panels Open Frame Rack No barrier, equipment fully exposed Best Use Case Cabinet favors shared or public-facing spaces Feature Accessibility Rack Cabinet Access through front and rear doors Open Frame Rack Access from any open side Best Use Case Open frame favors frequent maintenance access Feature Capacity Rack Cabinet Similar U capacity, added weight from panels Open Frame Rack Similar U capacity, lighter frame weight Best Use Case Both support 42U to 48U configurations Feature Ideal Environment Rack Cabinet Offices, colocation suites, mixed-use rooms Open Frame Rack Data centers with controlled room access Best Use Case Cabinet suits public buildings, open frame suits secure facilities What Are the Main Parts of a Rack Server? The main parts of a rack server include the internal hardware that performs computing tasks and the rack-mounted accessories that support installation, power distribution, cooling, and maintenance. Internal components handle processing, memory, storage, networking, and data protection, while supporting hardware secures the server inside the rack and improves accessibility. Together, these components enable reliable performance, efficient cooling, and simplified management across enterprise and data center environments. The main parts of a rack server deployment are listed below. Mounting Rails: Mounting rails attach to vertical posts inside the frame, supporting server chassis through fixed or sliding installation. Ball-bearing sliding rails allow technicians to extend equipment forward for maintenance without full removal. Rail compatibility depends on server depth and rack post spacing set by the manufacturer. Power Distribution Unit (PDU): A PDU delivers electrical power from facility circuits to installed servers and networking equipment. Rack-mounted PDUs include multiple outlets, with metered or switched models adding remote monitoring and outlet-level control. Redundant PDU configurations protect equipment against a single power feed failure. Keyboard, Video, Mouse (KVM) switch: A KVM switch provides centralized console access to multiple servers through a single monitor, keyboard, and mouse connection. Technicians switch between connected servers without moving physical peripherals between machines. KVM switches reduce desk space requirements in facilities managing dozens of rack-mounted systems. Cable Management Arm: A cable management arm holds cabling in place as a server slides forward on rails, preventing cable strain or disconnection during maintenance. Arms attach to the rear of the chassis, routing power and data cables along a controlled path. Cable management arms reduce accidental disconnection risk during routine service work. Blanking Panels: Blanking panels fill unused rack space, blocking exhaust air from recirculating into cold aisle intakes. Panels install without tools in most enclosed cabinet designs, snapping into open rack unit slots. Facilities applying blanking panels consistently report improved airflow separation across occupied and unoccupied rack space. What Are the Essential Rack Server Parts? The essential rack server parts include a motherboard, Central Processing Unit (CPU), memory modules, storage drives, Power Supply Units (PSUs), cooling fans, Network Interface Cards (NICs), and Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) controllers working together inside a single chassis. Component selection determines processing capacity, storage throughput, and power redundancy available within a single rack unit. Configuration varies by workload, though most rack servers share the same core hardware categories. The essential rack server parts are listed below. Motherboard: The motherboard connects every internal component, routing power and data between the processor, memory, storage, and expansion cards. Rack server motherboards use compact form factors to fit within 1U or 2U chassis height. Manufacturers design motherboards to support dual processors and high memory capacity for enterprise workloads. CPU: A CPU executes computing instructions across applications, operating systems, and virtualized workloads running on the server. Rack servers commonly support one or two CPUs per chassis, depending on socket count. Processor selection affects core count, clock speed, and total power draw within the rack. Memory Modules: Memory modules store active data temporarily, feeding information directly to the processor during operation. Rack servers support multiple memory slots, ranging from 8 to 64 slots depending on chassis size. Total memory capacity directly affects how many virtual machines or applications a server runs simultaneously. Storage Drives: Storage drives hold persistent data through hard disk drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), or Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) modules installed in front-facing bays. Drive count per chassis ranges from 2 to 24 bays, depending on server model and intended workload. RAID configurations across multiple drives protect data against single drive failure. Power Supply Units (PSUs): PSUs convert facility alternating current (AC) power into direct current (DC) power used by internal components. Rack servers commonly include redundant PSUs, allowing continued operation if a single unit fails. Redundant configurations connect to separate power feeds for added protection against circuit failure. Cooling Fans: Cooling fans pull air across internal components, directing heat from the processor and memory toward rear exhaust vents. Fan speed adjusts automatically based on internal temperature sensors, increasing airflow during peak load. Redundant fan arrays prevent thermal shutdown if a single fan fails during operation. Network Interface Cards (NICs): NICs connect a server to network switches, transmitting data at speeds reaching 10, 25, 100, 200, or 400 gigabits per second. Multiple NIC ports support redundant network paths, protecting against a single connection failure. Server workloads requiring high throughput often deploy multiple NICs in a single chassis. Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) Controllers: RAID controllers manage data distribution across multiple storage drives, balancing performance, redundancy, and capacity based on the configured array level. Hardware RAID controllers offload processing from the main CPU, improving storage performance under heavy load. Common configurations include RAID 1, RAID 5, and RAID 10, each offering different redundancy tradeoffs. How Are Rack Servers Installed in a Server Rack? Rack servers are installed into a Server Rack by following a defined hardware sequence, moving from frame preparation through component mounting and final cable connection. Technicians install internal hardware before mounting the completed chassis, or install pre-configured servers directly onto rack rails. Correct sequencing reduces installation time and prevents component damage during handling. Rack servers are installed into a Server Rack through the steps listed below. Install the Motherboard. Installing the motherboard first secures the primary circuit board to standoffs inside the chassis, aligning port openings with the rear panel. Technicians ground themselves before handling the board, preventing electrostatic discharge damage to onboard components. Install the CPU. Installing the CPU into its socket requires aligning notches correctly before locking the retention mechanism. Thermal paste application between the CPU and heat sink transfers heat efficiently once the system powers on. Install Memory Modules. Installing memory modules into designated slots requires matching module type and speed to motherboard specifications. Modules lock into place with a firm push until side clips engage automatically. Install Storage Drives. Installing storage drives into front-facing bays connects each unit to the backplane through a tool-less carrier or screwed bracket. RAID configuration occurs after physical installation, once the controller recognizes all connected drives. Install Power Supplies. Installing PSUs into rear bays connects internal power distribution to the motherboard and storage backplane. Redundant units slide into place, locking automatically to allow hot-swap replacement without shutting the server down. Install Cooling Fans. Installing cooling fans into designated bays connects each unit to the internal backplane or motherboard fan connector for speed control. Fan orientation matches the front-to-back airflow path used across most rack server designs. Install Network Interface Cards. Installing NICs into expansion slots connects the server to switch ports through copper or fiber cabling. Card seating requires firm, even pressure to avoid damaging the expansion slot connector. Install RAID Controllers. Installing a RAID controller into an expansion slot or onboard socket connects storage drives through dedicated data cabling. Configuration through firmware or software defines the array level applied across connected drives. How Do You Mount Rack Servers Safely? You mount rack servers safely by following proper lifting technique, rail alignment, and weight distribution guidelines during installation. Heavier equipment mounted too high raises tip risk and complicates maintenance access. Facilities following manufacturer weight and clearance guidelines reduce injury risk and equipment damage during installation. Rack servers mount safely through the steps listed below. Attach Mounting Rails First. Attaching mounting rails to both the server chassis and rack posts before lifting equipment prevents misalignment during installation. Rail spacing must match the depth setting recorded on the rack specification sheet. Use Lifting Equipment for Heavy Units. Using a mechanical lift or a second technician for chassis exceeding 18 kilograms (40 pounds) prevents back strain and dropped equipment. Two-person or mechanical lifts apply to many fully populated 2U and larger chassis models. Mount Heavier Equipment Lower. Mounting heavier equipment near the bottom of the frame lowers the center of gravity, reducing tip risk during rack movement or servicing. Lighter switches and patch panels install higher in the frame without stability concerns. Secure Fasteners Completely. Securing every mounting screw or cage nut before releasing lift support confirms the chassis sits fully supported by the rail system. Loose fasteners create vibration risk during ongoing server operation. How Do You Organize Cables Inside a Server Rack? You organize cables inside a Server Rack by separating power and data pathways, labeling every connection, and maintaining proper bend radius throughout installation. Poor routing blocks intake vents and complicates identification of individual connections during service work. Structured cabling practices reduce downtime risk tied to accidental disconnection or airflow restriction. Cables are organized inside a Server Rack through the steps listed below. Separate Power and Data Cabling. Separating power and data cabling into distinct pathways reduces electromagnetic interference between circuits. Vertical cable managers on opposite sides of the rack keep each cable type isolated. Label Every Connection. Labeling every cable at both ends identifies source and destination points without tracing the full run manually. Color-coded labels speed troubleshooting across racks containing dozens of connections. Maintain Proper Bend Radius. Maintaining a bend radius of at least four times the cable diameter prevents internal conductor damage and signal degradation. Sharp bends near connectors create the highest failure risk over time. Route Cables Away From Airflow Paths. Routing cables through side channels or overhead trays keeps front and rear airflow paths clear of obstruction. Blocked vents raise intake temperature and reduce cooling efficiency across mounted equipment. How Are Server Racks Used in Data Centers? Server Racks organize compute, storage, and networking equipment into standardized rows across a data center floor, supporting structured airflow and power distribution. Facilities arrange racks in aisles, pairing equipment fronts toward cold aisles and equipment backs toward hot aisles to separate chilled supply air from warm exhaust. Row spacing typically measures 900 millimeters to 1,200 millimeters (3 to 4 feet), meeting clearance requirements for maintenance access and airflow volume. Power distribution to each rack runs through overhead busways or under-floor conduit, feeding redundant PDUs mounted within the frame. Network cabling connects rack-mounted switches to core infrastructure through structured cabling paths, minimizing latency between compute and storage tiers. Full-size deployments commonly reach 42U to 48U per rack, supporting dozens of 1U or 2U servers within a single footprint. Data center operators monitor rack-level temperature, humidity, and power draw continuously, feeding data into Data Center Infrastructure Management (DCIM) platforms to detect developing issues before failure occurs. What Is a Data Center Rack? A data center rack is a standardized frame installed within a dedicated facility, holding servers, switches, and storage arrays under controlled temperature and humidity conditions. Frames follow the same EIA-310 sizing standard applied across enterprise and colocation environments, typically reaching 42U to 48U in height. Facility-grade racks often include reinforced construction, higher weight capacity, and integrated cable management compared to office-grade frames. Colocation providers lease rack space by the unit or by the full frame, billing customers based on power draw and occupied rack units. Redundant power feeds and structured cabling paths distinguish data center racks from standalone office installations. Environmental monitoring at rack level tracks temperature, humidity, and airflow continuously across facility operations. How Are Server Racks Arranged in a Data Center? Server Racks are arranged in organized rows that support efficient airflow, power distribution, and maintenance across the data center floor. Most facilities follow a hot aisle and cold aisle layout, positioning server fronts toward cold aisles to receive cooled air while directing warm exhaust toward hot aisles. Consistent row spacing also provides sufficient clearance for technicians, equipment installation, and cooling systems. Containment systems, including aisle doors and ceiling panels, help prevent hot and cold air from mixing in high-density environments. Facilities often position higher-density racks closer to dedicated cooling infrastructure to maintain consistent operating temperatures and improve cooling efficiency throughout the Data Center. While structural standards like EIA-310 keep server dimensions consistent, real-world data center design comes down to simple airflow and load management. Keeping cool air separated from hot exhaust and placing heavy gear low in the rack prevents basic thermal and balance issues before they start. Practical server room reliability is mostly about doing these simple layout fundamentals right every single time. Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering How Do You Choose the Right Server Rack? You choose the right Server Rack by evaluating equipment size, power requirements, cooling capacity, available floor space, security requirements, and future expansion plans before installation. Every deployment has different capacity and environmental requirements, making rack selection an important part of long-term infrastructure planning. Choosing a rack that matches current workloads while allowing room for future growth improves scalability, maintenance efficiency, and overall system reliability. The right Server Rack is chosen through the steps listed below. Measure Available Space. Measuring floor space, ceiling height, and doorway clearance confirms a chosen frame physically fits the intended installation location. Depth requirements often exceed initial estimates once cable management and airflow clearance factor into the calculation. Calculate Required Capacity. Calculating required rack units (U) based on planned equipment count prevents undersized purchases that force early replacement. Adding 20% to 30% spare capacity accommodates future hardware additions without a second frame purchase. Confirm Power and Cooling Compatibility. Confirming available power circuits and cooling capacity at the installation site prevents overloading facility infrastructure once equipment powers on. High-density configurations may require dedicated circuits beyond standard office wiring. Select Frame Type and Security Level. Selecting between open frame, enclosed cabinet, or specialty construction depends on physical security needs and airflow priorities established earlier in planning. Facilities with public access typically require locking enclosed cabinets over open frames. Verify Weight and Load Rating. Verifying static and rolling load ratings against total planned equipment weight confirms the frame supports fully populated capacity. Enterprise racks commonly rate from 500 kilograms to 1,500 kilograms (1,100 pounds to 3,300 pounds) static load. Which Server Rack Size Should You Choose? The appropriate Server Rack size depends on the number of rack units required, equipment depth, available installation space, and future expansion requirements. Rack height is measured in rack units (U), where 1U equals 1.75 inches (44.45 mm). Organizations should select a rack that accommodates existing equipment while reserving additional capacity for future deployments. The most common server rack sizes are listed below. 6U to 12U: Suitable for small offices, branch locations, retail environments, and network closets supporting switches, routers, and compact servers. 18U to 24U: Suitable for medium-sized businesses requiring multiple servers, UPS systems, and networking equipment within limited floor space. 27U to 36U: Suitable for growing server rooms that require additional capacity for compute, storage, and network infrastructure. 42U: The industry-standard size for enterprise data centers because it balances equipment density, accessibility, and airflow efficiency. 45U to 48U: Suitable for high-density environments requiring maximum equipment capacity while maintaining the same floor footprint as standard enterprise racks. Which Factors Should You Consider Before Buying a Server Rack? You should consider budget, power availability, cooling compatibility, and long-term scalability before buying a Server Rack. Overlooking any single factor risks costly retrofits once equipment installs and operational demands increase. Reviewing each factor before purchase protects against undersized or incompatible frame selection. Factors to consider before buying a Server Rack are listed below. Budget Range: Budget range determines available frame quality, material construction, and included accessories at time of purchase. Open frame racks typically cost [$200 to $800], while enclosed cabinets range from [$500 to $5,000] depending on size and security features. Power Capacity: Power capacity available at the installation site limits total equipment load a single rack safely supports. Circuits rated below equipment power draw force load balancing across multiple racks or facility upgrades. Cooling Compatibility: Cooling compatibility between chosen equipment density and available airflow or liquid cooling infrastructure prevents thermal issues after installation. High-density deployments exceeding 15 kilowatts per rack often require liquid cooling support unavailable in standard air-cooled rooms. Cable Management Needs: Cable management needs grow alongside port count and connection complexity across installed equipment. Frames lacking integrated management accessories require aftermarket vertical and horizontal cable organizers. Future Scalability: Future scalability determines whether a chosen frame accommodates additional equipment without requiring full replacement within 3 to 5 years. Modular rack designs allow incremental capacity additions as equipment count grows. What Are the Best Practices for Managing a Server Rack? Server rack management combines organized equipment placement, structured cabling, airflow optimization, continuous monitoring, and physical security to maintain reliable infrastructure throughout the equipment lifecycle. Following consistent management practices simplifies maintenance, improves troubleshooting, reduces cooling inefficiencies, and minimizes the risk of unexpected downtime. Proper documentation also helps technicians manage equipment changes and future capacity planning more effectively. Best practices for managing a Server Rack are listed below. Label Equipment and Cabling. Labeling every device, port, and cable run at installation prevents confusion during future maintenance or troubleshooting. Consistent labeling conventions across a facility speed identification during multi-rack incidents. Standardize Rack Layout. Standardizing equipment placement and weight distribution across every rack simplifies troubleshooting and reduces installation errors between technicians. Heavier equipment positioned near the bottom of each frame keeps a consistent, predictable layout facility wide. Maintain Physical Security. Maintaining locked cabinet doors and restricted access logs protects installed equipment from tampering or unauthorized removal. Access records support incident investigation when equipment goes missing or configuration changes without documentation. Document Configuration Changes. Documenting every configuration change, firmware update, and hardware swap creates a reliable record for future troubleshooting. Change logs reduce diagnostic time when new issues surface after a recent modification. How Do You Improve Server Rack Cooling and Airflow? You improve Server Rack cooling and airflow by pairing structural airflow management with routine equipment maintenance across every mounted device. Sealed gaps and consistent airflow orientation prevent warm exhaust air from mixing with cold supply air entering server intakes. Facilities apply these steps alongside broader Data Center Cooling practices built around Cooling and Airflow. Server Rack cooling and airflow improve through the steps listed below. Install Blanking Panels. Installing blanking panels across unused rack space prevents warm exhaust air from recirculating into cold aisle intakes. Sealed gaps improve airflow separation and reduce cooling energy waste. Route Cables Away From Vents. Routing cables through side channels or overhead trays keeps front and rear vent openings clear of obstruction. Blocked vents raise intake temperature and reduce cooling efficiency across mounted equipment. Maintain Front-to-Back Airflow Orientation. Maintaining consistent front-to-back intake and exhaust orientation across every mounted device prevents conflicting airflow direction within the same Server Rack. Mixed orientation forces adjacent equipment to draw in already-heated exhaust air. Monitor Rack-Level Temperature. Monitoring temperature at rack inlets and outlets confirms equipment operates within the 18°C to 27°C range recommended by the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE). Sensor alerts flag drift before airflow issues affect equipment reliability. How Do You Maintain Server Rack Reliability and Uptime? You maintain Server Rack reliability and uptime by implementing redundant power systems, continuous environmental monitoring, preventive maintenance, and accurate equipment documentation. Applying these practices consistently reduces hardware failures, minimizes service interruptions, and improves long-term operational stability across rack-mounted infrastructure. Reliable maintenance procedures also help organizations identify potential issues before they affect business operations. Server Rack reliability and uptime maintained through the steps listed below. Deploy Redundant Power Feeds. Deploying dual PDUs connected to separate electrical circuits protects installed equipment against a single power feed failure. Redundant configurations allow continued operation during circuit maintenance or a utility disruption. Install an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). Install a UPS to provide backup power during utility outages, providing runtime for graceful shutdown or generator transfer. Battery capacity determines available runtime before equipment requires shutdown. Schedule Preventive Maintenance. Scheduling fastener checks, fan replacement, and firmware updates on a fixed interval extends equipment service life and reduces unplanned failure risk. Quarterly service intervals suit most enterprise deployments. Track Maintenance History. Tracking maintenance history, component age, and past failures across every rack supports accurate forecasting of replacement timelines. Documentation gaps delay root cause analysis during recurring equipment issues. Disclaimer The content appearing on this webpage is for informational purposes only. Standardized rack dimensions allow hardware from different manufacturers to fit within the same framework, improving equipment compatibility, airflow management, cable organization, and maintenance efficiency. Most enterprise server racks follow the Electronic Industries Alliance (EIA)-310 standard, which specifies a mounting width of 19 inches. Server racks are measured using rack units (U), where one rack unit equals 1.75 inches (44.45 millimeters (mm)) of vertical mounting space. Server rack deployments support equipment organization, standardized hardware installation, power distribution, cable management, and cooling efficiency across enterprise, colocation, and hyperscale facilities. Rack selection depends on equipment size, weight capacity, cooling requirements, security needs, and future expansion plans. What Is a Server Rack? A server rack is a standardized metal frame built to hold servers, switches, patch panels, and other IT hardware in an organized vertical structure. Manufacturers construct racks from steel or aluminum, following the EIA-310 standard that sets a nominal mounting width of 19 inches. Rack height is measured in rack units, with 1U equal to 1.75 inches (44.45 mm), letting operators calculate equipment capacity before installation. Data centers, network closets, and office server rooms rely on racks to consolidate hardware, reduce cabling distance, and simplify power distribution. Mounting rails inside the frame support sliding or fixed installation of rack-mount servers, while vertical space above and below equipment accommodates cable management arms and blanking panels. Full-size racks commonly reach 42U to 48U, holding dozens of 1U or 2U servers within a single footprint. Open frame designs expose equipment directly to room airflow, while enclosed cabinets add doors, side panels, and locking mechanisms for physical security. Selection of a specific frame depends on floor space, cooling method, and equipment density planned for the deployment. What Is the Difference Between a Server Rack and a Data Rack? Server Rack and data rack terminology overlaps significantly across the IT industry, with vendors and technicians often using both terms for the same physical frame. The distinction between the two centers on scope, since data rack sometimes covers networking, storage, and telecom equipment beyond server hardware alone. Rack units (U) measure vertical space inside a rack frame, with each U equal to 1.75 inches (44.45 mm) of mounting height. Manufacturers label server chassis, switches, and storage enclosures by U count, letting technicians match equipment to available rack space before ordering hardware. A 1U server occupies a single unit, a 2U chassis occupies two units, and full-size racks commonly span 42U to 48U in total height. Rack units matter because capacity planning, airflow design, and equipment compatibility depend on accurate U measurements. Miscalculating available U space leads to failed installations or wasted rack capacity, since a 4U chassis cannot fit inside a 2U opening regardless of width compatibility. Data center operators track U allocation across every rack to forecast growth, plan power distribution, and avoid overloading a single frame with equipment exceeding its rated capacity. Standardized U measurements let vendors design equipment compatible across different rack manufacturers, since the EIA-310 specification governs both width and unit height industry wide. Manufacturers group frames into open structures, enclosed structures, and specialty structures, each suited to different security and airflow requirements. Selection depends on floor space, access control, and environmental conditions present at the installation site. Server Rack types fall into the categories listed below. Open Structures: Open structures expose mounted equipment directly to room airflow, relying on two or four vertical posts without side panels. Frames in this category prioritize ventilation and low material cost over physical security. Open structures suit controlled-access facilities where airflow ranks above enclosure protection. Enclosed Structures: Enclosed structures surround equipment with side panels and lockable doors, adding a physical barrier against unauthorized access. Perforated panels maintain airflow while restricting tampering with installed hardware. Enclosed structures suit shared offices and mixed-use facilities requiring equipment protection. Specialty Structures: Specialty structures address unique installation conditions, including wall mounting, seismic reinforcement, or portable deployment. Frame dimensions and bracing differ from standard floor-mounted racks to meet site-specific constraints. Specialty structures suit branch offices, earthquake zones, and temporary or mobile deployments. What Are the Most Common Server Rack Types? The most common Server Rack types include open frame racks, enclosed cabinets, wall-mounted racks, and seismic racks, each suited to different security and installation needs. Selection depends on facility access control, available floor space, and regional building requirements. Facilities combine multiple types across a single deployment based on equipment sensitivity and location. The most common Server Rack types are listed below. Open Frame Racks: Open frame racks expose mounted equipment directly to room airflow, using two or four vertical posts without side panels or doors. Technicians access cabling and hardware from any side, simplifying installation and maintenance in controlled environments. Data centers with restricted room access commonly deploy open frames to maximize airflow and lower equipment cost. Enclosed Cabinets: Enclosed cabinets surround mounted equipment with side panels, front, and rear doors, adding locking mechanisms for physical security. Perforated doors allow airflow while blocking unauthorized access to installed hardware. Office environments and shared facilities favor enclosed cabinets to protect equipment from dust, tampering, and unauthorized removal. Wall-Mounted Racks: Wall-mounted racks attach directly to a wall surface, holding smaller equipment loads in space-limited environments. Capacity typically ranges from 4U to 24U, supporting switches, patch panels, and small servers. Branch offices and network closets rely on wall-mounted racks when floor space remains unavailable for a full-size frame. Seismic Racks: Seismic racks add reinforced framing, bracing, and anchoring points designed to withstand earthquake activity without equipment displacement. Construction follows standards including Telcordia GR-63-CORE, part of the Network Equipment-Building System (NEBS) compliance framework. Facilities located in earthquake-prone regions install seismic racks to protect hardware and maintain uptime during seismic events. How do rack cabinets and open frame racks compare? Rack cabinets and open frame racks differ primarily in airflow management, physical security, and equipment accessibility across a facility. Cabinets add enclosed panels and doors, trading airflow volume for protection against dust and unauthorized access. Open frames maximize airflow and access at the cost of physical security, favoring environments with restricted room entry. The main parts of a rack server include the internal hardware that performs computing tasks and the rack-mounted accessories that support installation, power distribution, cooling, and maintenance. Internal components handle processing, memory, storage, networking, and data protection, while supporting hardware secures the server inside the rack and improves accessibility. Together, these components enable reliable performance, efficient cooling, and simplified management across enterprise and data center environments. The main parts of a rack server deployment are listed below. Mounting Rails: Mounting rails attach to vertical posts inside the frame, supporting server chassis through fixed or sliding installation. Ball-bearing sliding rails allow technicians to extend equipment forward for maintenance without full removal. Rail compatibility depends on server depth and rack post spacing set by the manufacturer. Power Distribution Unit (PDU): A PDU delivers electrical power from facility circuits to installed servers and networking equipment. Rack-mounted PDUs include multiple outlets, with metered or switched models adding remote monitoring and outlet-level control. Redundant PDU configurations protect equipment against a single power feed failure. Keyboard, Video, Mouse (KVM) switch: A KVM switch provides centralized console access to multiple servers through a single monitor, keyboard, and mouse connection. Technicians switch between connected servers without moving physical peripherals between machines. KVM switches reduce desk space requirements in facilities managing dozens of rack-mounted systems. Cable Management Arm: A cable management arm holds cabling in place as a server slides forward on rails, preventing cable strain or disconnection during maintenance. Arms attach to the rear of the chassis, routing power and data cables along a controlled path. Cable management arms reduce accidental disconnection risk during routine service work. Blanking Panels: Blanking panels fill unused rack space, blocking exhaust air from recirculating into cold aisle intakes. Panels install without tools in most enclosed cabinet designs, snapping into open rack unit slots. Facilities applying blanking panels consistently report improved airflow separation across occupied and unoccupied rack space. What Are the Essential Rack Server Parts? The essential rack server parts include a motherboard, Central Processing Unit (CPU), memory modules, storage drives, Power Supply Units (PSUs), cooling fans, Network Interface Cards (NICs), and Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) controllers working together inside a single chassis. Component selection determines processing capacity, storage throughput, and power redundancy available within a single rack unit. Configuration varies by workload, though most rack servers share the same core hardware categories. The essential rack server parts are listed below. Motherboard: The motherboard connects every internal component, routing power and data between the processor, memory, storage, and expansion cards. Rack server motherboards use compact form factors to fit within 1U or 2U chassis height. Manufacturers design motherboards to support dual processors and high memory capacity for enterprise workloads. CPU: A CPU executes computing instructions across applications, operating systems, and virtualized workloads running on the server. Rack servers commonly support one or two CPUs per chassis, depending on socket count. Processor selection affects core count, clock speed, and total power draw within the rack. Memory Modules: Memory modules store active data temporarily, feeding information directly to the processor during operation. Rack servers support multiple memory slots, ranging from 8 to 64 slots depending on chassis size. Total memory capacity directly affects how many virtual machines or applications a server runs simultaneously. Storage Drives: Storage drives hold persistent data through hard disk drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), or Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) modules installed in front-facing bays. Drive count per chassis ranges from 2 to 24 bays, depending on server model and intended workload. RAID configurations across multiple drives protect data against single drive failure. Power Supply Units (PSUs): PSUs convert facility alternating current (AC) power into direct current (DC) power used by internal components. Rack servers commonly include redundant PSUs, allowing continued operation if a single unit fails. Redundant configurations connect to separate power feeds for added protection against circuit failure. Cooling Fans: Cooling fans pull air across internal components, directing heat from the processor and memory toward rear exhaust vents. Fan speed adjusts automatically based on internal temperature sensors, increasing airflow during peak load. Redundant fan arrays prevent thermal shutdown if a single fan fails during operation. Network Interface Cards (NICs): NICs connect a server to network switches, transmitting data at speeds reaching 10, 25, 100, 200, or 400 gigabits per second. Multiple NIC ports support redundant network paths, protecting against a single connection failure. Server workloads requiring high throughput often deploy multiple NICs in a single chassis. Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) Controllers: RAID controllers manage data distribution across multiple storage drives, balancing performance, redundancy, and capacity based on the configured array level. Hardware RAID controllers offload processing from the main CPU, improving storage performance under heavy load. Common configurations include RAID 1, RAID 5, and RAID 10, each offering different redundancy tradeoffs. How Are Rack Servers Installed in a Server Rack? Rack servers are installed into a Server Rack by following a defined hardware sequence, moving from frame preparation through component mounting and final cable connection. Technicians install internal hardware before mounting the completed chassis, or install pre-configured servers directly onto rack rails. Correct sequencing reduces installation time and prevents component damage during handling. Rack servers are installed into a Server Rack through the steps listed below. Install the Motherboard. Installing the motherboard first secures the primary circuit board to standoffs inside the chassis, aligning port openings with the rear panel. Technicians ground themselves before handling the board, preventing electrostatic discharge damage to onboard components. Install the CPU. Thermal paste application between the CPU and heat sink transfers heat efficiently once the system powers on. Install Memory Modules. Installing memory modules into designated slots requires matching module type and speed to motherboard specifications. Modules lock into place with a firm push until side clips engage automatically. RAID configuration occurs after physical installation, once the controller recognizes all connected drives. Install Power Supplies. Installing PSUs into rear bays connects internal power distribution to the motherboard and storage backplane. Redundant units slide into place, locking automatically to allow hot-swap replacement without shutting the server down. Install Cooling Fans. Installing cooling fans into designated bays connects each unit to the internal backplane or motherboard fan connector for speed control. Fan orientation matches the front-to-back airflow path used across most rack server designs. Install Network Interface Cards. Installing NICs into expansion slots connects the server to switch ports through copper or fiber cabling. Card seating requires firm, even pressure to avoid damaging the expansion slot connector. Install RAID Controllers. Installing a RAID controller into an expansion slot or onboard socket connects storage drives through dedicated data cabling. Configuration through firmware or software defines the array level applied across connected drives. How Do You Mount Rack Servers Safely? You mount rack servers safely by following proper lifting technique, rail alignment, and weight distribution guidelines during installation. Heavier equipment mounted too high raises tip risk and complicates maintenance access. Facilities following manufacturer weight and clearance guidelines reduce injury risk and equipment damage during installation. Rack servers mount safely through the steps listed below. Attach Mounting Rails First. Attaching mounting rails to both the server chassis and rack posts before lifting equipment prevents misalignment during installation. Rail spacing must match the depth setting recorded on the rack specification sheet. Use Lifting Equipment for Heavy Units. Using a mechanical lift or a second technician for chassis exceeding 18 kilograms (40 pounds) prevents back strain and dropped equipment. Two-person or mechanical lifts apply to many fully populated 2U and larger chassis models. Mount Heavier Equipment Lower. Mounting heavier equipment near the bottom of the frame lowers the center of gravity, reducing tip risk during rack movement or servicing. Lighter switches and patch panels install higher in the frame without stability concerns. Secure Fasteners Completely. Securing every mounting screw or cage nut before releasing lift support confirms the chassis sits fully supported by the rail system. Loose fasteners create vibration risk during ongoing server operation. How Do You Organize Cables Inside a Server Rack? Structured cabling practices reduce downtime risk tied to accidental disconnection or airflow restriction. Cables are organized inside a Server Rack through the steps listed below. Vertical cable managers on opposite sides of the rack keep each cable type isolated. Label Every Connection. Labeling every cable at both ends identifies source and destination points without tracing the full run manually. Color-coded labels speed troubleshooting across racks containing dozens of connections. Maintain Proper Bend Radius. Maintaining a bend radius of at least four times the cable diameter prevents internal conductor damage and signal degradation. Sharp bends near connectors create the highest failure risk over time. Which Factors Should You Consider Before Buying a Server Rack? You should consider budget, power availability, cooling compatibility, and long-term scalability before buying a Server Rack. Overlooking any single factor risks costly retrofits once equipment installs and operational demands increase. Reviewing each factor before purchase protects against undersized or incompatible frame selection. Factors to consider before buying a Server Rack are listed below. Budget Range: Budget range determines available frame quality, material construction, and included accessories at time of purchase. Open frame racks typically cost [$200 to $800], while enclosed cabinets range from [$500 to $5,000] depending on size and security features. Power Capacity: Power capacity available at the installation site limits total equipment load a single rack safely supports. Circuits rated below equipment power draw force load balancing across multiple racks or facility upgrades. Cooling Compatibility: Cooling compatibility between chosen equipment density and available airflow or liquid cooling infrastructure prevents thermal issues after installation. High-density deployments exceeding 15 kilowatts per rack often require liquid cooling support unavailable in standard air-cooled rooms. Cable Management Needs: Cable management needs grow alongside port count and connection complexity across installed equipment. Frames lacking integrated management accessories require aftermarket vertical and horizontal cable organizers. Future Scalability: Future scalability determines whether a chosen frame accommodates additional equipment without requiring full replacement within 3 to 5 years. Modular rack designs allow incremental capacity additions as equipment count grows. What Are the Best Practices for Managing a Server Rack? Server rack management combines organized equipment placement, structured cabling, airflow optimization, continuous monitoring, and physical security to maintain reliable infrastructure throughout the equipment lifecycle. Following consistent management practices simplifies maintenance, improves troubleshooting, reduces cooling inefficiencies, and minimizes the risk of unexpected downtime. Proper documentation also helps technicians manage equipment changes and future capacity planning more effectively. Best practices for managing a Server Rack are listed below. Label Equipment and Cabling. Labeling every device, port, and cable run at installation prevents confusion during future maintenance or troubleshooting. Consistent labeling conventions across a facility speed identification during multi-rack incidents. Standardize Rack Layout. Standardizing equipment placement and weight distribution across every rack simplifies troubleshooting and reduces installation errors between technicians. Heavier equipment positioned near the bottom of each frame keeps a consistent, predictable layout facility wide. Maintain Physical Security. Maintaining locked cabinet doors and restricted access logs protects installed equipment from tampering or unauthorized removal. Access records support incident investigation when equipment goes missing or configuration changes without documentation. Document Configuration Changes. Documenting every configuration change, firmware update, and hardware swap creates a reliable record for future troubleshooting. Change logs reduce diagnostic time when new issues surface after a recent modification. How Do You Improve Server Rack Cooling and Airflow? You improve Server Rack cooling and airflow by pairing structural airflow management with routine equipment maintenance across every mounted device. Sealed gaps and consistent airflow orientation prevent warm exhaust air from mixing with cold supply air entering server intakes. Facilities apply these steps alongside broader Data Center Cooling practices built around Cooling and Airflow. Server Rack cooling and airflow improve through the steps listed below. Install Blanking Panels. Installing blanking panels across unused rack space prevents warm exhaust air from recirculating into cold aisle intakes. Sealed gaps improve airflow separation and reduce cooling energy waste. Route Cables Away From Vents. Routing cables through side channels or overhead trays keeps front and rear vent openings clear of obstruction. Blocked vents raise intake temperature and reduce cooling efficiency across mounted equipment. Maintain Front-to-Back Airflow Orientation. Maintaining consistent front-to-back intake and exhaust orientation across every mounted device prevents conflicting airflow direction within the same Server Rack. Mixed orientation forces adjacent equipment to draw in already-heated exhaust air. Monitor Rack-Level Temperature. Monitoring temperature at rack inlets and outlets confirms equipment operates within the 18°C to 27°C range recommended by the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE). Sensor alerts flag drift before airflow issues affect equipment reliability. How Do You Maintain Server Rack Reliability and Uptime? You maintain Server Rack reliability and uptime by implementing redundant power systems, continuous environmental monitoring, preventive maintenance, and accurate equipment documentation. Applying these practices consistently reduces hardware failures, minimizes service interruptions, and improves long-term operational stability across rack-mounted infrastructure. Reliable maintenance procedures also help organizations identify potential issues before they affect business operations. Server Rack reliability and uptime maintained through the steps listed below. Deploy Redundant Power Feeds. Deploying dual PDUs connected to separate electrical circuits protects installed equipment against a single power feed failure. Redundant configurations allow continued operation during circuit maintenance or a utility disruption. Install an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). Install a UPS to provide backup power during utility outages, providing runtime for graceful shutdown or generator transfer. Battery capacity determines available runtime before equipment requires shutdown. Schedule Preventive Maintenance. Scheduling fastener checks, fan replacement, and firmware updates on a fixed interval extends equipment service life and reduces unplanned failure risk. Quarterly service intervals suit most enterprise deployments. Track Maintenance History. Tracking maintenance history, component age, and past failures across every rack supports accurate forecasting of replacement timelines. Documentation gaps delay root cause analysis during recurring equipment issues. Disclaimer The content appearing on this webpage is for informational purposes only. Any performance parameters, geometric tolerances, specific design features, quality and types of materials, or processes should not be inferred to represent what will be delivered by third-party suppliers or manufacturers through Xometry’s network. Buyers seeking quotes for parts are responsible for defining the specific requirements for those parts. Please refer to our terms and conditions for more information. events.before: Resources / Industry Design / Inspection Options Inspection Options Written by Greg Paulsen 4 min read Published October 8, 2020 Updated August 26, 2026 Xometry offers industry-standard inspection options through our instant quoting engine. Xometry's Inspection Services Xometry offers inspection as part of the Instant Quoting Engine . These can include formal inspection reports, CMM measurements of GD&T dimensions, source inspection, and more. Each inspection offering and its definition and which processes it applies to are detailed below. Xometry's Inspection Selections Standard Inspection QC will verify that the part material, features, and finish are in accordance with the part requirements specified in the quote, CAD file, and/or print. If no dimensional print is provided with a part, QC measures to Xometry's Manufacturing Standards on dimensions they deem critical, such as overall size, holes, and depths. If a dimensional print is provided, QC will verify up to 20 dimensions they deem critical. Documentation will not be shipped with your parts. Formal Inspection with Dimensional Report QC will perform an inspection using calibrated tools where 100% of all dimensions, attributes, dimensional locations, and print notes will be documented per our Statistical Sampling Plan based on ASQC Z1.4 2008 Level II with Zero rejects. A dimensional inspection report with a correlated ballooned print will be shipped with your part(s). A customer-supplied dimensional print is required for this inspection. The number of inspection points is subject to the applicable 100 maximum. Greater quantities require a Custom Inspection and additional charges. CMM Inspection with Dimensional Report QC will perform an inspection using a Coordinate Measurement Machine (CMM) where 100% of all dimensions, attributes, dimensional locations, and print notes will be documented per our Statistical Sampling Plan based on ASQC Z1.4 2008 Level II with Zero rejects. A dimensional report with a correlated ballooned print will be shipped with your part(s). A customer-supplied dimensional print is required for this inspection. The number of inspection points is subject to the applicable 100 maximum. Greater quantities require a Custom Inspection and additional charges. First Article Inspection Report (FAIR AS9102) QC will perform a First Article Inspection per the requirements specified in SAE Aerospace Standard (AS 9102) documentation (or equivalent). The purpose of the First Article Inspection is to provide objective evidence that all engineering design and specification requirements are properly understood, accounted for, verified, and documented. QC will maintain a quality record for customer review of accountability and planning, for performing periodic surveillance and audits to verify conformance, for evaluating root cause and corrective action for any non-conformances, and for problem investigations. A dimensional report with a correlated ballooned print will be shipped with your part(s). Random sampling is based on ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 Level II to an Acceptance Quality Level (AQL) of 2.5%. A customer-specified dimensional print is required for a First Article Inspection. We will build the full lot and do the FAI form at the final QC treating this lot like the first Article. If you want a 1 part and stop for approval, please select custom inspection. The number of inspection points is subject to the applicable 100 maximum. Greater quantities require a Custom Inspection and additional charges. Source Inspection A Source Inspection audit is an inspection of purchased products and process records at the supplier's premises to verify compliance with requirements before shipment to the customer. A Source Inspection can include but is not limited to requirements review, specification compliance, and a quality review of the manufacturer. A source inspection will be scheduled based on the order lead time and when parts are ready to ship. The order will ship after the source inspection is complete. A customer-supplied dimensional print is required for this inspection. Custom Inspection Choose this option if your part requires other inspection requirements such as, but not limited to, the following: Non-Destructive Testing, Serialization, Custom Sampling Plan, or if you would like to provide your own inspection datasheet. A customer-supplied dimensional print is required for this inspection. events.before: Resources / Injection Molding / Managing Sink in Injection Molding Designs Managing Sink in Injection Molding Designs Written by Greg Paulsen 3 min read Published October 9, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 Reduce divots and see-thru marks on your molded part with these tips. What is Sink? A thick section between a boss and the outer wall causing significant sink marks Sink is one of the most common cosmetic defects in injection molded parts, and is characterized by surface depressions, often in sections with thick walls. This is caused by the uneven shrinking of material as it cools, when thicker cross-sections of a part pull more than the thinner areas when hardening from liquid to solid, leaving divots on the opposite side. An example of this is when there are ribs or boss (screw mount) features on the opposite side of a cosmetic face. Sink from ribs will appear as lines or a grid impression, and a boss may make little dips akin to a doughnut shape. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Ways to Mitigate Sink Sink is not inherently bad. But if the part has cosmetic requirements, it may be unappealing. The good news is that sink can usually be mitigated through best design practices. Here are three go-to rules for managing sink in your next injection molded project. 1. Make all your outer walls uniform. This design strategy, in addition to designing internal ribs that are 40-60% of the outer wall thickness, will help manage sink in your injection molded parts. To see this in practice, take a look at a LEGO or pop off the battery cap of your remote to see this in practice. The outer wall of a part is its primary structure, and also where the material will flow with the least resistance—filling the part cavity in the mold. Ribs are used to add strength and rigidity without adding excess thickness. However, note that ribs that are the same thickness as a wall tend to show more sink because they are pulling material away from the wall and into the rib when cooling. By making ribs thinner than the outer walls, the outer walls will actually stay more stable than the rib, which will significantly reduce sink marks. 2. Cut some material away from boss features. This is a really interesting trick that can remove visible rings from a cosmetic face. A boss is a cylinder extruded out, typically perpendicular, from a surface. It has an interior hole which will usually accommodate a thread, an insert, or a screw for assembly. Using the rule above, the boss should have a nominal thickness of 40-60% of the outer wall. In addition, the thickness ratio between the internal blind hole and the outer wall should be at the same 40-60% range. The last feature is a triangular groove around the boss which is 30% of the wall thickness deep and merging back to the outer wall at a 30-degree angle. These additional cuts reduce and move the points of mass which would traditionally pull material while cooling, thus mitigating sink marks. Removing material around a boss will reduce the see-thru of sink on the opposite side 3. Adding texture to the cosmetic surface. Even with best design practices, there may still be faint sink marks visible on the surface. Using a matte surface finishing such as mold texturing (MT-11010, MT-11020, or the equivalent), or SPI matte finishes like C3 to D3, will help hide any remaining sink marks by reducing glare pick up from minor imperfections. This includes a detailed injection molding design guide and live engineering support to get free and direct help on your injection molding quote.
